title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
summary: Opens the practice section. Sādhanā joins body, mind and breath; the learner keeps a simple, disciplined life and an attitude of faith rather than envy, and trains three things: breath through prāṇāyāma, the tongue through the syllables ṭa and ka, and the fingers through exercise.

prev.title: The Sound of the Bīn from the Bānsurī

blocks.verse:
सकारेण शरीरः स्याद् धकारो भवेत्।
नकारेण स्मृतः प्राणः साधना त्रिगुणात्मिका।६०।
blocks.text: By the syllable sa the body is meant; dha [stands for concentration]; by na the life-breath is understood: [so] sādhanā has the nature of the three guṇas.

Broadly, the meaning of sādhanā is the activity that leads from ignorance towards knowledge. Even so, here the author's own intent is given, which is set out in this śloka on the basis of scientific truth. Until body, mind and prāṇa (life-breath) are brought in one direction and one sets out from comfort towards discomfort, there can be no sādhanā of any subject. So, (sa) for śarīra (body), dha for dhāraṇā (concentration) and na for prāṇa: thus, by including body, mind and prāṇa in sādhanā, sādhanā has been described as having the three guṇas, sattva, rajas and tamas.

blocks.verse:
युक्ताहार विहाराभ्याम ब्रम्हचारि व्रते स्थितः।
प्राण जिह्वांगुलीयांञ्च साधयेद् धैर्य पूर्वकम।६१।
blocks.text: Through balanced āhāra and vihāra, and keeping to the vow of brahmacarya, one should patiently train the breath, the tongue and the fingers.

That is, delighting in the five objects taken in through the body's five organs of knowledge is called āhāra (intake), and the activities done through the five organs of action are called vihāra (conduct). To sift these two through far-sightedness and fine discernment and to keep the mind in control over them is itself a yoga. Practice of the bānsurī too is not possible without yoga.

Along with this, to remove the natural restlessness of the mind, it will be necessary to look upon the various feelings towards many many-coloured things and persons, in the light of knowledge, with a sense of oneness. The essence of all things and persons seen in this way is called Brahman. One who moves the mind in That is called a brahmacārī. To take care of the body's subtle but precious element, that is to protect the vīrya (semen), is also a principal part of brahmacarya (continence, discipline). In common usage a one-sided form of brahmacarya is current; in the sādhanā (practice) of the bānsurī this is necessary.

So, by reforming āhāra and vihāra in this way, try to bring simplicity into life. Then, while keeping brahmacarya, one should practise the prāṇa (breath), jihvā (tongue) and fingers by the methods below. Bear in mind that with a feeling of śraddhā (reverence) sādhanā becomes easy, whereas with a feeling of envy sādhanā becomes harsh. A feeling of hatred or envy towards any person, or of greed for any thing or position, arises of itself. To regard these as destroyers of the yajña (sacrifice) of sādhanā and to disregard them, and to keep setting up again and again in the mind the feeling of reverence towards knowledge, is the sādhaka's mental yajña.

blocks.verse:
प्राणस्य सोधयेन्मांर्गम् पूरक कुम्भक रेचकैः।
टकावुच्यार्य जिह्वांश्च व्यायामेनांगुलीयकान्।६२।
blocks.text: One should purify the path of the breath by pūraka, kumbhaka and recaka (inhalation, retention and exhalation); the tongue by pronouncing ṭa and ka; and the fingers by exercise.
That is, one should perfect the prāṇa (breath) by prāṇāyāma (breath control), the tongue by ṭa and ka, and the fingers by vyāyāma (exercise).
